title: The best images from Mercedes' title celebrations
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli might have sealed the drivers' title in Mexico City, but it took one race longer for Mercedes to claim their ninth Constructors' Championship title.

The Silver Arrows won the teams' title in Sao Paulo, courtesy of George Russell's fourth-place finish, with Antonelli in fifth. That was more than enough to beat Ferrari, who had both cars down the order.

As such, Mercedes took their first constructors' title since 2021, and the celebrations at track were special. After seeing Red Bull win in 2022 and 2023, and then McLaren take back-to-back titles, Mercedes were clearly very, very happy to be back at the pinacle of the sport.

title: Rivals congratulate Mercedes on Constructors' Championship
excerpt:
Mercedes' wait for another Constructors' Championship ended last weekend, as the German manufacturer achieved the feat at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

The Silver Arrows only needed to outscore main rivals Ferrari by a handful of points in Brazil, with P4 for George Russell and P5 for new World Champion Kimi Antonelli proving more than enough.

The title is Mercedes' first as a team since 2021, while the success in 2026 brings their total count up to nine constructors' titles, joint with Williams and third behind only Ferrari (16) and McLaren (10).

"I'm so proud for the organisation," said Team Principal Toto Wolff after the race in Brazil.

"We've taken a few years to be back on the top spot. Not many teams have been able to come back from such a situation.

"And it just shows that, you know, the great work, the great people that we have in our organisation. And it's fantastic to be among them."

Mercedes' success came under the new-for-2026 regulations, which included drastic overhauls to both the aerodynamics and power units of the cars.

Mercedes' Trackside Engineering Director Andrew Shovlin admitted that "we've never put so much effort into a new set of regulations" before.

He said: "We had periods where it looked like we were going to get there [win another title], and then you weren't, and you have all these setbacks. When you've finally done it again, it's just immensely satisfying.

"And, you know, no one gave up. They just kept pushing, kept working hard. There was obviously a big rule change this year. We've never put so much effort into a new set of regulations."

Rivals up and down the grid offered their congratulations to the new World Champions, including McLaren, the Woking-based outfit having lost their crown from last season.

All the key moments from the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix

McLaren CEO Zak Brown posted on X: "Congratulations to Mercedes and HPP on securing the Constructors’ Championship title after an impressive season. Looking forward to fighting you for it again next year."

Team Principal Andrea Stella added during a post-race media session: "[I want to] congratulate Mercedes on winning the Constructors’ Championship. Formula 1 is operating, like I've been saying for some time, at very, very high level, very high standards.

"So to be able to win in this kind of competitive context is a reflection of great work that must have happened at Mercedes, so they deserve to be certainly acknowledged."

Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton, who won six of his seven drivers' titles with Mercedes and was at the team as it won eight consecutive teams' titles, posted on Instagram: "Congratulations guys, am so happy for you all. So well deserved."

Red Bull Team Principal Laurent Mekies added in his post-race media session: "I think they have done an outstanding job. We all recall how dominant they were at the start of the season.

"And of course, we knew they had switched earlier than most [last year to focus on 2026], but it's something to switch earlier than most, something else to convert it into lap time, and that's what they have done.

"And you know they started the season with more than a second advantage on us, so they have obviously done a very good job, so well done to them."

Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali also gave his congratulations to the latest winners in the championship.

“My huge congratulations to everyone at the Mercedes Formula 1 Team on becoming 2026 Constructors’ World Champions. Reaching the summit of Formula 1 is never the achievement of one person alone," he said.

"It is the result of extraordinary talent, relentless determination and the shared belief of hundreds of people, at the circuit and back at the factory, all united by the same ambition. Every single member of this team should feel incredibly proud of what they have achieved.

"This is also a moment that will have a special place in the history of our sport. With his ninth Constructors’ title, my friend Toto Wolff draws level with the great Sir Frank Williams, one of Formula 1’s true legends. To stand alongside Frank in the record books is an extraordinary achievement and a powerful testament to Toto’s leadership, vision and relentless pursuit of excellence over so many years.

"To win the Constructors’ Championship in the same season that Kimi Antonelli became the youngest ever Drivers’ World Champion makes 2026 truly unforgettable for Mercedes and for Formula 1. This is what our sport is all about: dreaming big, pushing beyond the limits, and proving what is possible when great people come together with one shared purpose.

"Mercedes have returned to the very top, and in doing so have written another remarkable chapter in the history of Formula 1.”

title: How Verstappen outperformed Red Bull’s simulations in Brazil
excerpt:
The Sao Paulo Grand Prix was a superb race for Red Bull Racing as Max Verstappen put in an extraordinary charge from 21st on the grid to second, and Isack Hadjar backed him up with a solid third place.

What made Verstappen’s progress through the field so impressive was that the man himself had cautioned that with the 2026 cars, passing would not be as easy as he had previously demonstrated at Interlagos.

And yet he somehow found the performance that he needed, even if at times he made it clear that he wasn’t happy with the balance of the RB22.

Team Principal Laurent Mekies confirmed that the Dutchman had outperformed Red Bull’s pre-race expectations.

“As always, I think no sim in the world would predict that you go from P21 to P2, or that you get 14 places in five laps,” he said. “There is no sim being able to do that. So he's beating the sim on a regular basis!”

The obvious disappointment was that Verstappen had to start from the back of the grid, something that was not anticipated going into the weekend.

“Of course it's frustrating, because the pace seemed good on Friday and also on Saturday morning, and in some respects in Q1 when we let him qualify,” said Mekies.

“But it's part of the game. It's easy to forget, it's the first year with the power unit, and the guys have been doing an extraordinary job. And we take the first penalty with Max this weekend, and that's what it is. It was not planned. We had a small issue on Friday that forced us to do so.”

Intriguingly Mekies conceded that it was not a given that Verstappen could have beaten winner Lando Norris, even if he’d started at the sharp end.

“Well done to Lando and to McLaren,” said the Frenchman. “I think they were generally a bit faster than us in the race. I also think that even if you start P2, say, I think on pace Lando was anyway a bit a bit faster than us.

“So of course it's a different story if you start P2, because you have all the first opening laps risk taking, on which Max is unbelievable. But I think they were a bit faster than us.”

Mekies couldn’t say definitively why that was: “Is it degradation? Is it pure pace? Obviously, they brought another fair bit of upgrade this weekend again. Or is it something else?

“Because you may have heard Max being fairly vocal with the car balance once we had switched to dry tyres, and from that point onward, he has been very, very unhappy with car balance, including when we came back to the inters at the very end.

“So we need to analyse what happened there, how much of that is time loss, and whether or not that would have been enough to fight with McLaren.”

On his charge through the field, Verstappen was helped by Hadjar letting him through. Mekies admits that there was an option to swap the places back later on, but it didn’t happen.

Verstappen reflects on 'challenging' P21 to podium charge

“I think we would have done it if the cars had stayed close together,” he noted. “We would have done it, because Isack had a very strong pace and he stayed with Max, as you have seen after the swap.

“But then, as the race panned out and the rain came again, the cars were very, very distant, and it would not have made sense. Plus, increased rain intensity at the end, it would not have made any sense. But I have to say, Max and Isack worked very, very strongly together to give us that result.”

Hadjar may have been disappointed not to have been able to finish ahead of his team mate, but nevertheless Interlagos was another strong performance, making good progress after struggling to find the right setup earlier in the weekend.

“I think ultimately, if you ask me right now, I think it's the best race he has done with us in terms of pure pace, and that's what we look at,” said Mekies. “Pure pace on the dries, on the inters, super difficult conditions, in how clever he has been racing. He has done a lot of very strong racing this year, but I think he has raised the bar another time.

“So that's what we want to keep seeing. That's what we said we were most impressed by when we took the decisions to confirm him for '27, the way he keeps raising the bar, and we were simply hoping to provide him with the environment for him to keep doing that. I think he has done that today in terms of the race, and in the context where he has been building through the weekend.”

A win for McLaren coming just a week after an event that saw Ferrari on pole and in contention for victory was another sign of just how competitive F1 currently is at the front of the grid, with the top four teams evenly matched.

“The convergence is probably happening earlier than what we all thought,” said Mekies. “I'm guessing somehow it's perhaps an indication of fairly restrictive regulations. That being said, you see cars with visibly different concepts, and you see four top teams fighting, which is probably a great point to be for the sport.

“So, let's see how it will pan out in the second year. But it's fair to say that having to be already in the second part of '26 in the situation where you turn up at the race weekend, and you don't know which one of the four top teams is going to win the race, I think it's great for the sport.

“And yes, we get now top five in Qualifying separated by two-tenths, and it's a strong combination of development race and absolute perfect execution if you want to win on Sunday.”

title: Stella reveals how McLaren triumphed at Interlagos
excerpt:
The Sao Paulo Grand Prix was a race of tyres and the challenge getting them into the right window, whether they be the intermediates used at the start and finish, or the soft slicks deployed in the middle part of the race.

Lando Norris and McLaren did a better job than anyone else across a very difficult afternoon of changing conditions, and they reaped the reward with a superb victory.

Team Principal Andrea Stella conceded that the cooler conditions in Interlagos on Sunday tipped the balance in favour of the MCL40.

"My explanation of our performance in dry today is associated with the track and ambient temperature,” said the Italian post-race.

“The conditions were very cold, much colder than we had in practice. In practice, I think we saw that we were still tending to overheat the tyres. Today, somehow the conditions came our way, and we could keep the tyre temperature under control. I think that's the main reason.

“We know that we have some work to do in terms of getting more consistent in long runs in hot conditions, and I think we were in a way helped.

“You could see also this well, especially with Lando, when the track was getting greasy before switching onto intermediate tyres. Lando was just able to keep the lap times much better than anybody else, and I think our car is good from this point of view."

It wasn’t entirely straightforward, however. Stella noted that some cars were more competitive at various stages of the afternoon.

“I think what we have seen is that cars exhibited different features,” he said. “Like at the start of the race, you needed to be good at bringing the tyres into temperature.

“In the laps to the grid, nobody could actually generate any temperature. So definitely, in the early laps, there was a premium to the cars, or the drivers, that were able to generate tyre temperature.

“Obviously Max [Verstappen], likewise Lewis [Hamilton], I think they have shown their talent not only from a tyre switching on point of view, but also in the first lap. I watched some images; they were just incredible how easily they gained positions.

“But going back to the evolution of the race, I think something we have seen [Saturday], even in Qualifying, we seemed to be good when there was a lot of water, and then we kind of lost it a little bit in Q2 when there was less water.

“Likewise today, it was difficult to see a car that was good in all conditions. We struggled a bit more with Lando at the start, and then somehow we managed to keep good grip in the intermediate tyres, and also on the soft tyres.

“I think in the final part of the stint on the soft tyres, Lando was very fast, and probably there he is the one that had done the best job. Because if you look at [Kimi] Antonelli as well, he was good at the final part of the stint on soft, and he struggled at the start, and he lost position.

“So, it was technically a very interesting race, because really everyone had to deal at some stage with the tyres being either too cold or getting too hot, but without a clear pattern. All teams will have some data to look into, and understand.”

One of the intriguing aspects of the race came in the slick tyre stint, as drivers discussed the possibility of running to the end on their original set, with Norris and McLaren among those to have such a conversation.

However as those who changed to fresh rubber showed good pace, rivals were obliged to follow suit.

“Antonelli decided to go for another stop, and this made our life a little easier from this point of view,” said Stella. “I don't think at any stage we thought that we could have gone all the way to the end.

“Russell, I think, is the only one that took advantage for staying on the same set and going on to intermediate tyres. This was a consideration, but we were unsure as to how the rain would have actually manifested itself. So we decided with both drivers to go for the more rational approach, which was just go on another set.”

Norris delighted to 'give back' to McLaren in Sao Paulo win

It wasn’t all about tyres, however, and Stella paid tribute to Norris, who has a great feel for low grip conditions.

“You're never going to have a really perfect car, you're never going to have the perfect conditions,” said Stella. “So adaptability is actually probably the most important feature that you may want to possess as a driver.

"I think that should be definitely acknowledged and recognised for Lando, when there's a need to understand what's best, how to operate, he is definitely a master.

“Hopefully we don't need to rely on these qualities though, we just want to make sure that we can offer Lando and Oscar [Piastri] a competitive car such that they can just drive a little bit more easily, because still our car remains pretty difficult.”

Norris won twice in the summer at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort, and he looked set to triumph in Madrid before getting caught out by the Virtual Safety Car. Since then, McLaren have been outperformed by their rivals, and thus a victory late in the season was most welcome.

It bodes well for the Interlagos upgrade package, the first part of a step towards the 2027 car that the team has fast tracked for this season.

“As for the McLaren trajectory, after the upgrades in Hungary, it was encouraging that we were in position to win,” said Stella. “We should have won Madrid, really. But after that, other people took upgrades, and we lost this position. I think we also paid the price on not having had great Qualifying sessions.

“It would have been interesting to see Lando starting from the front in races like Austin or Mexico. I think it would have been definitely a fight for podium, but it's thanks to these upgrades that we are now in condition to fight for the victory, combined with the conditions surely.”

There’s more to come for the next race: “And these upgrades, first of all, they will be complemented by some more parts that come in Vegas, and they form the foundation for what will be next year's car.

“So it's encouraging for the trajectory of McLaren that we seem to be able to transform our development into performance on track, and it's also important for McLaren that we had solid pit stops because we don't come from a period of consistent pit stops, and also execution in these mixed conditions.

“Because we have had some disappointing races, like in Canada, where we were starting with the intermediate tyres, and the double extra formation lap was unlucky, honestly.

"So it's good that we were able to master these conditions at the pit wall as well. And I'm very proud to have seen the team operate at this very high level.”

title: Piastri and management team mutually terminate agreement
excerpt:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri has split from his management team, led by nine-time Grand Prix winner Mark Webber and his partner Ann Webber.

A joint statement on the Monday after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix said the two sides had "mutually agreed to terminate their management agreement".

Nine-time winner Piastri, who is competing in his fourth season in F1, said: "I'd like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years.

"Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward."

Former Red Bull, Williams and Jaguar driver Mark Webber added: "We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar's career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early on.

"Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close.

"This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career."

Norris wins Sao Paulo GP thriller as Mercedes claim title

The Webbers started working with Piastri in 2019, when the Australian won his first single-seater championship with victory in the Formula Renault Eurocup as well as securing a spot on the Renault F1 Team's junior programme.

The 25-year-old went on to win the FIA Formula 3 Championship title the next season and followed that up with a title win in the FIA Formula 2 Championship in 2021.

Renault's rebranded Alpine team squandered the chance to promote Piastri from reserve to a full-time race seat, leaving the door open for the Australian to find a seat elsewhere.

Mark Webber opened talks with McLaren and secured a deal for Piastri to make his F1 debut with the British team in 2023 as a replacement for fellow Australian Daniel Ricciardo.

It proved a decisive move for the Australian's career. Piastri took two podiums in his rookie season and secured his first Grand Prix win the following year in Hungary.

Piastri then launched an impressive title charge in a third campaign with McLaren in 2025 before ultimately losing out to team mate Lando Norris.

The Webbers took a step back from a front-line role with Piastri this year and went from having a regular presence at track to only making fleeting appearances.

Piastri's former race engineer at Prema, Pedro Matos, and his mental coach, Emma Murray, have since taken on a greater role at track as part of the Australian's close team.

And as per the statement on Monday, Piastri – who currently sits seventh in the Drivers' Championship – will operate under a new management structure going forward.

title: Vasseur explains Ferrari’s tyre struggles in Brazil
excerpt:
The Sao Paulo Grand Prix represented a disappointing weekend for Ferrari.

P8 and P9 in the final classification at Interlagos for Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton showed just how difficult an event it was for a team that was disappointed to finish a close second in Mexico City just a week earlier.

In the end, the Sao Paulo result was impacted more by tyres than anything else, as not for the first time in 2026 the team struggled to get into right temperature window.

Both drivers went into the weekend knowing that they would face 10-place grid hits for taking new power unit elements, and then life was made even harder for Hamilton when an issue with his new engine in FP3 triggered a further change for Qualifying.

Only the fact that other drivers also had big penalties saw him start P20 rather than dead last, while Leclerc dropped down to P14 having originally qualified fourth.

The start was perhaps the highlight of the team’s weekend as Hamilton gained 11 places on the first lap as he charged up to an astonishing ninth place, although a few laps later had to give a spot back to Ollie Bearman for making the move off track.

However, by then he was already in trouble as he struggled to keep his intermediates in the right window, while Leclerc had similar issues, and wasn’t making much progress.

Hamilton’s tyre frustration led him to call for a change to slicks, and he was the first driver to make the switch. However, he still struggled to get the dry tyres to work, and after surviving a spin when the rain returned, he eventually finished ninth.

Leclerc did at least find some pace in the late stages, but was a little too eager to get by Liam Lawson for P7. Having made contact just before completing the pass he received a penalty that dropped him back a place in the final classification.

Team Principal Fred Vasseur confirmed that tyres had dominated Ferrari’s Sunday.

“I don't want to speak in details of technical stuff,” said the Frenchman. “But for sure it's a lot about tyre temperature, and in certain phases of the race or certain conditions we are struggling more.

“And yeah, there was a huge gap between the beginning of the stint of Charles on softs and last couple of laps, when he was almost as fast as the guys with new tyres.

Leclerc and Hamilton lament 'horrendous' Sao Paulo GP

“As usual, when you have an issue with tyres, the effect or the impact is always much, much higher than the characteristic of the car, or the upgrade that you bring. You can bring an upgrade a weekend, if you are not in the right spot with the tyres, you are nowhere because the magnitude of this is half a second, but most of the upgrades or the characteristic of the track is tenths.”

The team only briefly got it right in Interlagos: “This weekend I think we were able to be into the pace on some occasions, and some occasions we were far away.

“Then there is another issue – starting from the back with the penalty, and the fact that we are still struggling in terms of top speed. When you have only one line dry, it's mega difficult, and we are stuck at the back.”

Vasseur conceded that the team were always on the back foot thanks to the grid penalties.

“On Friday we knew that, and then when you have to take the penalty, the approach of the weekend is a bit different.

“Friday we struggled. Saturday was much better, both conditions [dry FP3 and wet Qualifying], but I think it's an accumulation between the mix of the top speed issue, we had to put the tyres in temperature, and we are at the back, and we are struggling. And then we are trying to find a shortcut on the strategy, and so on.”

Regarding Hamilton’s insistence on going to slicks early he said: “If you have a look, Alonso was faster on the lap after with the inter. I think we anticipated when we pitted Lewis – it was to be aggressive, and perhaps a bit too much.”

Brazil saw Mercedes claim the 2026 Constructors’ Championship, leaving Ferrari in a distant second. The wait for the first Maranello title since 2008 continues.

“I think everybody on the grid wants to win, wants to fight,” said Vasseur. “And we are all competitors, and we all want to win. When you start the championship, you have this goal.

“Now we knew from the beginning that it would be difficult for us, we understood from the first straight line, and I think the team did a good job to continue to push to develop the engine.

“I think on the chassis side, on the grip limited side, we are more than performant. But yeah, for sure, congratulations to Mercedes – and see you next year!”

excerpt:
Max Verstappen has a history of big Brazilian comebacks, but on Saturday night he was talking down his chances of contending for victory from a penalised 21st on the grid.

This wasn’t a new situation for Verstappen – he won there from 17th in 2024, and last year he came from the pit lane to the podium – but the Dutchman was less confident of a comeback at this year’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

title: All the key moments from the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix
excerpt:
Lando Norris claimed victory in a wet thriller at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, while Mercedes did enough to secure the 2026 Constructors' Championship.

There were plenty of story lines up and down the grid, including a runner-up finish for Max Verstappen after starting at the back of the grid, while the wet weather gave midfield runner Liam Lawson the chance to shine.

Here are all the key moments from the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix…

Norris overcomes the weather to make it back-to-back Sao Paulo wins

Interlagos proved to be a happy hunting ground for Norris last season, the McLaren driver taking victory 12 months ago en route to the title at the end of the season.

Having taken back-to-back wins in the summer this term, Norris and McLaren had failed to feature in the lead battle of recent Grands Prix due to a lack of outright pace, but the combination looked strong in Brazil's dry practice running.

That pace translated over to the wet as well, with Norris claiming pole during Saturday's thunderstorms as he looked like a genuine contender for victory no matter the elements.

The Briton's task became harder, though, as he immediately lost his advantage to fellow front row starter Kimi Antonelli off the line, and lost a further spot through the opening corners to Lawson.

Recovering P2 as Lawson's intermediate tyres overheated, Norris pitted a lap earlier than Antonelli for slick rubber, slashing a 7s gap in the process and, shortly after, forcing the Mercedes driver into a spin at Turn 1.

Thereafter, Norris controlled the pace at the front of the field, managing tricky conditions in the final stages after switching to intermediate tyres and claiming his third win of the season by 14s from Verstappen.

“The main thing today was I just kept it cool and I didn't make any mistakes," said Norris. "I had the pace when I needed to, so it was good. Nice to be back on the top step, and what a place to do it as well.”

Norris delighted to ‘give something back’ to McLaren with Sao Paulo win

Mercedes clinch constructors’ title despite spins for Russell and Antonelli

Mercedes entered the weekend all but assured of claiming a constructors' title for the first time since 2021, just one weekend after Antonelli claimed his maiden drivers' crown.

The Italian was outpaced, however, by team mate George Russell in the wet Qualifying session, as the pair finished second and third quickest.

Russell had been left annoyed after missing out on pole when backing out of his lap in the best of the conditions, but the Briton had to serve a five-place grid penalty for an Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) change, dropping him to P7 on the grid.

There was drama even before the start for Antonelli, with the new World Champion running wide at Turn 12 on his reconnaissance lap and spinning his car on the grass, before scrambling back to the pits undamaged.

As Antonelli grabbed the lead at the start, Russell worked his way up the order and pitted from P4 as drivers moved to slick tyres, only for him to spin on the damp pit exit.

After recovering to point the right way, Russell continued on the fringes of the top 10, while Antonelli lost his lead to Norris after a spin of his own at Turn 1.

Antonelli would lose further places after running wide at the opening corner to the Red Bull duo, while rain in the closing stages meant a stop for intermediate tyres, with Russell allowed to pass his team mate for P4.

Antonelli finished P5 and remained there despite being handed a five-second penalty post-race for an unsafe pit release at his final stop, the result not denying Mercedes this year's title.

Verstappen completes another epic Sao Paulo recovery

It was yet another epic recovery drive from Verstappen in Sao Paulo as the Red Bull driver stormed to the podium from the back of the grid.

He had taken a penalty after having several power unit components changed on his car but sliced through the field in the opening laps, eventually finishing in P2.

Interlagos has proved to be a happy hunting ground for Verstappen in recent seasons, winning the 2024 Grand Prix in the wet from P17, and finishing third last year after starting in the pit lane.

It was a double podium for Red Bull too, with Isack Hadjar finishing in P3 – the second double of the season after the duo did the same in Baku.

Having started in P4, the Frenchman moved up to P2 during the middle section of the race but received team orders to let Verstappen by after running wide and losing time at Turn 1.

Verstappen reflects on 'challenging' Sao Paulo GP as he charges from P21 to the podium

Ferrari's 'complete disaster'

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton only scored six points between them, marking a disappointing race for Ferrari.

Hamilton had an impressive opening lap on his 400th F1 start, with an incredible charge through the field gaining him 11 places from his P20 grid position following his power unit grid penalties.

However, the performance of his intermediate tyres rapidly declined and he dropped back, hindered further by an investigation into him leaving the track and gaining an advantage, and a late spin – which all contributed to his P9 finish.

Meanwhile, Leclerc also had a grid drop penalty after replacing his ICE, but could not follow his team mate up the order in the opening laps.

He did gradually gain positions through the pit stops and switched to intermediate tyres at the right time, allowing him to cling on as the rain started to fall and eventually fight his way past Lawson for P7.

However, he was given a post-race five-second penalty for contact with the New Zealander, dropping him to P8 – with the Monegasque calling the day a “complete disaster”.

Lawson impresses yet again from the midfield

Lawson has been quietly putting together a very strong season for Racing Bulls, the Kiwi racer lying ninth in the standings, a long way clear of Pierre Gasly in P10.

His more than decent form was evident in Brazil, where he qualified fifth in Saturday’s rainstorm, showing he has what it takes in the wet before mixing it with the front runners from his P3 starting slot on Sunday, courtesy of grid penalties.

He overtook Norris on the opening lap as he got his elbows out, and even chased after Antonelli, before dropping back once the faster cars began to recover.

Nonetheless, he finished best of the midfield, showed his defensive skills in battling Leclerc late on to beat both Ferraris on a day where mistakes were easy to make. That scored his team more valuable points as they look to seal P5 in the teams’ standings.

Despite all of that, and despite having more than double the amount of points as his team mate Arvid Lindblad, Lawson is still not assured of his seat on the grid next year. Racing Bulls have yet to announce either driver for 2027, with Nikola Tsolov the man waiting in the wings.

Lawson has scored in 15 of the 20 Grands Prix contested so far this season, with a top finish of fifth back in Monaco. He even adapted well in his stint at Red Bull, jumping back up to the team in place of the injured Hadjar for three rounds, but whether all that is enough to secure a drive next season remains to be seen.

A contract extension for Interlagos as Brazil delivers another outstanding race

The Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace, better known as Interlagos, will be on the F1 calendar until at least 2035, something the drivers and fans have both rejoiced at.

That contract extension was announced ahead of a thrilling wet Qualifying session that saw the drivers show all their skills and no small amount of bravery as they barrelled around in treacherous conditions.

The Grand Prix delivered on action as well, with Verstappen once again carving his name into the record books with another superb recovery drive from the back all the way to P2. Hamilton also cut his way through early on, while there were spins, strategy dilemmas and plenty of overtakes to enjoy.

The track simply does not deliver straightforward Grands Prix, and with so many titles having been decided here down the years, it has seen the full range of emotions from some of the greats of the sport.

title: How Lawson stated his case with a brilliant Brazilian weekend
excerpt:
For Liam Lawson the Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend could hardly have gone any better, and the sight of a Racing Bulls car overtaking Lando Norris on the first lap to run in second place was something that nobody could have predicted.

While he would no doubt have liked to have finished higher up the order than the P7 that he ultimately earned, realistically it was never going to be easy to keep the cars from the four top teams behind him – even in a race impacted at both the start and finish by a damp track.

It was a superb P5 in Saturday’s Qualifying that set up Lawson’s strong race. Penalties for others promoted him to third on the grid, and from there a good start and a poor launch by Norris allowed him to get into second, behind only Kimi Antonelli.

However, his intermediates were soon past their best, and he dropped back behind Norris, Isack Hadjar, George Russell and Max Verstappen.

“I mean, crazy race,” he said. “Honestly, I had a really good start. Good grip in Turn 1. Obviously made up a place, and then to be honest, I was thinking I might try and attack Kimi at some point in the lap.

“But yeah, just once the pace stabilises, they're a lot quicker than us, and we started to pull back. We were damaging our tyre, I think, quite a lot more than them. And then I think the pace on the dry was okay.”

Lawson wasn’t the only driver to struggle as their intermediates got older in that opening stint, with Lewis Hamilton also falling away after his good opening run.

“I think it's a bit of graining,” said Lawson. “The problem is that you never know whether to push through the graining and try and wear it all off, or to try and look after the tyre and stop the graining."

“And when it's dry like this, you can't really do much. So for us, the graining started halfway through Lap 1, honestly. And I think for us, we were never really going to be able to keep those cars there anyway. So I'll go and review it, and see if there's something else I could have done.”

As the race progressed on slick tyres Lawson lost places to Oscar Piastri and a recovering Russell. When the rain returned in the closing laps he still had high hopes of hanging onto P7 on the road, but he lost out to a resurgent Charles Leclerc – who gave him a friendly nudge along the way.

“Then at the end, I tried to keep Charles there,” said Lawson. “We had some contact in [Turn] 12. I'll go and review it. I don't really know exactly what to say yet, but obviously I ended up losing the place.”

He also initially feared that he might pick up a puncture: “I think it was his wing that hit my tyre, so I think we got really lucky. I feel like it was exactly like his GP2 move in Abu Dhabi, on Albon years ago. He did the same kind of thing, so maybe it's his specialty. I don't know if it's legal or not! We'll obviously go and review it, but it was a good battle overall.”

The stewards duly decided it wasn’t legal, and gave Leclerc a penalty that promoted Lawson from his P8 at the flag back to P7.

“I feel like we maximised today,” Lawson continued. “I had a had a strong race. I would have liked it to stay wet the whole race. It would have been cool. I probably would have had more of a shot there. But at the moment, we're topping the midfield as a team, and that's what we're targeting every weekend.”

Indeed the points he earned have extended the healthy advantage Racing Bulls already had over Alpine in the battle for P5. However, he’s taking nothing for granted, despite the big gap.

“We've seen it before,” he said. “We had it here a few years ago with Alpine, so we're not going to settle until it's done. But we're in a great place. The car is very, very strong. A couple more races to go, so I'm excited to finish off the season.”

Regarding the Las Vegas Grand Prix, the next round on the calendar, he added: “I think there we're expecting Alpine to be quite strong. They're very, very quick down the straights. So I imagine they'll be strong there. So yeah, let's see.”

Meanwhile, like everyone else, Lawson is awaiting firm news on the 2027 Racing Bulls line-up, with Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings, and a decision promised soon by team boss Alan Permane.

“I appreciate all the support I'e seen over the last few weeks,” he said. “It's honestly really nice to see. Obviously, I would love it if it was more from a team! But at the moment, I'm just trying to enjoy driving the car because with everything else going on, I don't really know what else I'm meant to do.

“I don't know what else I'm meant to say to you guys. I'm just going to keep driving and yeah, see what happens. I feel like Alan's been extremely supportive to me, and I appreciate that a lot, and I have enjoyed working closely with them and with the team this year. But obviously it's a big organisation.”

title: McLaren react to Lando Norris champagne and 'pyrotechnics' issues
excerpt:
Andrea Stella has explained that Lando Norris was caught out by pyrotechnics during the podium celebrations after his São Paulo Grand Prix win, rather than his broken champagne bottle moment.

Norris claimed a dominant victory at Interlagos, crossing the line more than 14 seconds clear of Max Verstappen to take his third win of the season, and 14th of his F1 career.

But the celebrations on the rostrum took an unexpected turn. As Norris leapt off the dais, he first attempted to stoke up the champagne by hitting the bottle on the floor, only for it to smash and be left holding the neck.

The Briton then moved forward, only to be caught on the side of the head by the sparks from a sprinkler-style pyrotechnic effect firing at close range.

Later clarifying what had happened once Norris was back in the paddock, McLaren team principal Stella, speaking to media, including RacingNews365, said: "I understand that he had an incident with the pyrotechnics, not with the bottle," said Stella.

"Okay, I think the bottle didn't go well either because he seemed like he had only the upper part.

"But I think he was just surprised when he was going for the bottle. I understand that the pyrotechnics started.

"The only thing I needed to know is that he is okay."

[Article continues below]

Stella - 'Our car is good from this point of view'

Beyond the podium mishap, Stella also used his media session to address McLaren's pace through the race, pointing to the unusually cold conditions as a key factor behind the team's tyre management in the dry.

"My explanation of our performance in the dry is associated with the track and ambient temperature," explained Stella.

"The conditions were very cold, much colder than we had in practice. In those conditions in practice, I think we saw that we were still tending to overheat the tyres.

"Somehow the conditions came our way, and we could keep the tyre temperature under control. I think that's the main reason.

"We know that we have some work to do in terms of getting more consistent in long runs in hot conditions, and I think we were in a way helped.

"You could see this well when, especially with Lando, the track was getting greasy before switching onto intermediate tyres,

"Lando was just able to keep the lap times much better than anybody else, and I think our car is good from this point of view."

title: Max Verstappen jaw-dropping as Lewis Hamilton suffers - Sao Paulo GP Winners and Losers
excerpt:
Lando Norris converted pole position into victory at Interlagos, while a sensational recovery drive from Max Verstappen and a brief flash of brilliance from Liam Lawson lit up a chaotic, rain-affected São Paulo Grand Prix.

Mercedes, meanwhile, secured the constructors' championship without either driver reaching the podium, a quietly remarkable way to confirm the title.

It was a weekend that swung wildly in both directions, with Ferrari's race unravelling through mechanical misfortune and driver error, Cadillac suffering a mechanical failure before the race had even begun, and Gabriel Bortoleto's home race turning into a weekend to forget.

Check out RacingNews365's São Paulo Winners and Losers below!

Winner: Lando Norris

Norris did exactly what he needed to do, turning pole position into a comfortable, points-maximising victory.

The McLaren driver set the fastest time in qualifying and was never seriously troubled at the front, crossing the line well clear of Verstappen.

A poor start saw him slip to third going into the first corner but he eased back past Lawson, before a rare Kimi Antonelli spin saw him reclaim the lead. From then on, it was an easy afternoon.

It marks a truly positive result for the Briton and McLaren, who will aim to end the season on a high after what has been a challenging campaign.

© XPB Images

Loser: Lewis Hamilton

Hamilton produced one of the laps of the season on the opening lap, surging from 20th to ninth in his 400th grand prix start, before it all fell apart.

Ferrari had set his intermediate tyre pressures too aggressively, according to team principal Fred Vasseur, generating instant heat but triggering ballooning and rapid degradation within five laps.

A communication error from the pit wall then left him out on slicks as rain returned, resulting in a spin and a barrier brush at the final corner.

He eventually crossed the line a lap down in ninth, a result that flattered a genuinely torrid afternoon.

© XPB Images

Winner: Max Verstappen

Verstappen's charge from 21st to second was arguably the single most eye-catching achievement of the weekend.

The Red Bull driver gained nine positions on the opening lap alone in treacherous wet conditions, then timed his move to slick tyres cleanly as the track dried.

Isack Hadjar was instructed to hand back second place to his teammate on lap 38, after early leader Antonelli suffered multiple spins, clearing Verstappen's path to the podium.

He later admitted the car's balance felt completely different once on slicks, which stopped him from threatening Norris, but a podium from 21st on the grid was still a result few saw coming.

© Red Bull Content Pool

Loser: Valtteri Bottas

Bottas's weekend ended before it began. A cross-threaded, jammed right-rear wheel nut was discovered during pre-grid tyre changes, and Cadillac mechanics were unable to free it in time for the start.

The Finn, who had been cleared to race after a heavy suspension failure the previous week in Mexico, was forced to withdraw without turning a competitive lap.

For a team still searching for its first points of the season, a mechanical failure of this kind on the grid is about as deflating as it gets.

© XPB Images

Winner: Liam Lawson

Lawson delivered one of his strongest weekends of the season, qualifying a superb fifth before a penalty elsewhere promoted him to third on the grid.

He briefly ran in second place around Norris at the start, a remarkable sight for the Racing Bulls driver, before tyre degradation on his intermediates dropped him back through the order.

He recovered to finish sixth, later elevated from seventh after a five-second penalty for Charles Leclerc for a collision between the pair.

It capped a weekend in which Lawson looked genuinely competitive with the cars ahead of him, and further demonstrated his case for a fresh contract.

© XPB Images

Loser: Gabriel Bortoleto

Bortoleto's home race could hardly have gone worse. The Audi driver spun into the barriers during a wet Q1, taking the blame himself for the error, and compounded that with a 10-place grid penalty for fitting an additional energy store and control electronics unit.

He lost further ground at the start after being overtaken by Sergio Pérez, then struggled through mixed wet-dry conditions all afternoon.

He eventually finished 16th, a lap down, in front of his own fans at Interlagos, a result that will sting far more given the occasion.

Bonus Winner: Mercedes

Mercedes clinched the constructors' championship at Interlagos, ending a drought stretching back to 2021, and did so in understated fashion.

George Russell finished fourth and Antonelli fifth, marking the first race all season in which neither Mercedes driver reached the podium yet the team still walked away with the title.

The result underlined the consistency of the Mercedes-AMG F1 W17 E Performance package across a full campaign under the sport's 2026 technical regulations, rather than relying on a single standout weekend.

Clinching a championship without a podium finish is a rare feat, and it speaks to the depth of performance Mercedes has built across the grid this year.

title: George Russell walked out of FIA press conference: 'I thought, you need to chill'
excerpt:
George Russell walked out of a press conference before it had finished, after a qualifying session in Brazil left him fuming over a lost pole position.

The Mercedes driver finished second on the grid for the São Paulo Grand Prix, after his race engineer, Marcus Dudley, had told him to abort a lap after coming across the Williams of Alex Albon in the middle sector. Russell felt the lap was good enough for pole.

Moments later, the rain intensified, costing Russell what would have been his best shot at top spot.

The 28-year-old made his frustration clear over the radio, refusing to accept muted congratulations for his final position.

After berating Dudley, and then being told by team principal Toto Wolff he was P2, a furious Russell replied: "P2? I'm not here for second place; I'm here for first place," Russell said. "It was a lap good enough for P1."

That anger carried straight into the FIA press conference, according to host Tom Clarkson, who discussed the incident on the F1 Nation podcast.

"He actually walked out of the press conference while it was still going on," said Clarkson. "He was just done with it.

"I'd asked him a question about that lap that he didn't complete because he was told not to by his race engineer Marcus Dudley, and when he sort of had enough of answering questions, he just got up and walked out."

Clarkson did not hold back in his assessment of the Briton's state of mind at the time.

"I just came away thinking, George, you need to chill because this is going to start eating away at you," he said.

"And then in the race, we all saw what happened," referring to Russell's spin in the pit lane.

It was the second time in a week Russell had not fulfilled all of his media duties. In Mexico, after Kimi Antonelli had wrapped up his first F1 title, Russell avoided his post-race press obligations, citing "relentless" frustration at another result that went begging due to circumstances out of his control.

title: Red Bull reveal plan to impose team orders on Max Verstappen
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has confirmed Max Verstappen would have been instructed to hand second place back to Isack Hadjar during the São Paulo Grand Prix had the pair remained close enough on track.

Hadjar, who started fifth at Interlagos, was initially asked to let Verstappen through on lap 38, as the Dutchman charged through the field from P21 on the grid following a power unit penalty.

The decision was taken to allow Verstappen to chase race leader Lando Norris, who had established a lead of more than nine seconds.

However, Hadjar remained within a second of his team-mate and subsequently questioned whether the positions would be reversed if Verstappen could not catch the McLaren driver.

Mekies has now confirmed that Red Bull intended to facilitate another switch, but the changing conditions and differing strategies ultimately made that impractical.

"I think we would have done it," Mekies told media, including RacingNews365. "If the cars had stayed close together, we would have done it because Isack had a very strong pace and he stayed with Max, as you have seen, after the swap.

"But then, as the race panned out and the rain came again, the cars were very, very distant, and it wouldn't have made sense.

"Plus, with increased rain intensity at the end, it would not have made any sense."

[Article continues below]

A tricky subject at Red Bull

The willingness to potentially instruct Verstappen to surrender a position was notable, given Red Bull's tendency to impose team orders in favour of the four-time F1 drivers' champion rather than his team-mate.

The Dutchman caused a stir at Interlagos in 2022, when he refused to let Sergio Perez pass, despite having already wrapped up the title with his team-mate fighting to finish second in the standings.

More recently, Hadjar ruffled feathers at the United States Grand Prix in Austin, initially resisting an instruction to allow Verstappen through because he feared losing race time.

The Frenchman eventually acquiesced when his race engineer made clear he was being told to move aside, rather than asked.

In Brazil, however, Hadjar complied with the initial instruction without resistance and remained competitive before the two Red Bulls became separated as the race unfolded.

Verstappen ultimately finished second behind Norris, with Hadjar completing the podium in third, securing a double podium for Red Bull in the rain-affected 71-lap contest.

Reflecting on the performance, Mekies added: "But I have to say, Max and Isack worked very, very strongly together to give us the result."

title: Mercedes face 'interesting exercise' after Toto Wolff identifies 'something wrong'
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has conceded Mercedes may have got "something wrong" with its cars at the São Paulo Grand Prix after both George Russell and Kimi Antonelli complained of unusual handling during a chaotic race.

The pair finished fourth and fifth respectively in the 71-lap contest at Interlagos, securing Mercedes' ninth Formula 1 constructors' championship, and its first since 2021, despite struggling with the balance of their W17s.

Russell lost significant time when he spun at the pit-lane exit after changing from intermediate to slick tyres, briefly brushing the wall as he tried to recover. The mistake sent him tumbling down the order to P10 before he fought back to fourth.

Antonelli, meanwhile, led the opening stages but reported that something felt wrong with the car and suspected a suspension problem. He subsequently spun at Turn 1, surrendering the lead to Lando Norris, and later lost further positions, finishing fifth.

Mercedes could not immediately identify the cause of the unpredictable behaviour, although Wolff suspected the team's tyre pressures or set-up may have contributed.

"I think both have been given a very tricky car at times; George is not someone who spins in the pit lane on the exit, and Kimi is the same," Wolff told media, including RacingNews365.

"Both reported a very, very strange behaviour of the car, like something's broken on the suspension or too much pressure in the tyres.

"And whilst it was not only them, because Max said the same thing, I believe that we've gotten something wrong on the pressures or on the setup because now, looking at the cars, the rear tyres are also completely, completely worn — the fronts are like new, so there's something which we haven't spotted."

The Austrian nevertheless stressed that Mercedes had shown strong pace at certain points, leaving the team to investigate the inconsistency even as it celebrated clinching the title with three rounds remaining.

"But then at times in the race we were absolutely flying," the Mercedes team principal added.

"So we are walking away with an interesting exercise to find out what it was, but with a positive mindset after winning the constructors' championship."

title: Which has been Max Verstappen's best São Paulo GP drive over last three years?
excerpt:
This is a tough one for you to decide, so get voting!

Max Verstappen has turned Interlagos into his personal theatre of recovery over the past three seasons, producing three wildly different fightbacks at a circuit that keeps punishing him in qualifying and rewarding him on Sunday.

With the 2026 edition of the São Paulo Grand Prix now in the books, RacingNews365 wants to know which of the four-time F1 champion's three drives through the field stands above the rest.

© XPBimages

2024 - 17th to first

Verstappen's 2024 triumph came in atrocious conditions, with the race disrupted by heavy downpours, a virtual safety car, a full safety car and eventually a red flag.

Starting from 17th on the grid - a net 15th as Williams' Alex Albon and Lance Stroll in his Aston Martin did not start - Verstappen and Red Bull gambled by staying out on intermediate tyres through tricky rain fluctuations rather than pitting, building track position that paid off when the red flag allowed a tyre change without the usual pit-lane time loss.

From there, Verstappen picked off the leaders in the spray, eventually crossing the line more than 19 seconds clear of Esteban Ocon to claim a win that arguably did more than any other result that year to cement his fourth title.

He also took the fastest lap on the way to victory, a near-perfect execution of a changeable, chaotic afternoon.

© XPBimages

2025 - pit lane to third

A fresh Honda power unit fitted under parc fermé rules forced Verstappen to start the 2025 race from the pit lane.

Starting on hard tyres, his race was turned upside down again when a right-front puncture sent him in for an unplanned stop on lap six under a virtual safety car.

That early stop, however, shifted Verstappen onto an offset tyre cycle that let him spend most of the race on mediums, giving him a decisive pace advantage over rivals stuck on softs. A late stop for fresh softs let him attack and pass George Russell.

Verstappen conceded afterwards that he had not expected a podium when he woke up that Sunday morning, yet he finished third behind race winner Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli.

© Red Bull Content Pool

2026 - 21st to second

This year's edition produced arguably the most dramatic turnaround yet. Verstappen was shuffled to the back row of the field after Red Bull fitted power unit components beyond his seasonal allocation, incurring an aggregate 30-place grid penalty.

In a wet-dry-wet race, from 21st, Verstappen sliced through the field early on courtesy of a stunning first stint on inters. By lap eight, he was into the top six.

As the track dried, two stints on softs saw Verstappen eventually make his way up to second, despite feeling that something was "broken" in the car and heavily affecting its balance.

When the final inter stint commenced in earnest, Verstappen had a shot at victory as he was 7.5s behind McLaren's Lando Norris.

Whatever was the issue with the RB22, Verstappen was unable to replicate his opening spell on the green-striped Pirellis, finishing 14 seconds behind Norris at the flag. Regardless, it had been another masterful performance from the Dutchman.

So, three different penalties, three different strategies, three podium results. Which of these Interlagos drives deserves the title of Verstappen's best? Cast your vote!

title: 2026 F1 Sao Paulo Grand Prix Driver Ratings: See which drivers scored a 10
excerpt:
Check out the driver ratings from RacingNews365 from the 2026 F1 Sao Paulo Grand Prix in Brazil.

The rules have been broken in the RacingNews365 driver ratings for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

One driver's performance was so good that he earned a score reserved only for those who achieve something he didn't do.

Find out who it is below, in a high-scoring edition of driver ratings...

The top five

Lando Norris - 10

A tour de force from the outgoing world champion, whose only lost half-mark comes from losing a position off the start to the incoming one, Antonelli. Wins it back, though, through his dominance after getting the lead back on his way to a strong win. Stay away from champagne bottles and fireworks.

Max Verstappen - 10

A very rare occasion of a driver receiving a score of 10, despite not taking pole or winning the race. Would have been a contender for pole if there was any point in him making Q3, but there wasn't so he parked it in Q2 with the engine penalty. Thereafter, P21 to P2 was nothing less than expected, and the very idea it was even being floated pre-race speaks volumes. Could have given Norris a run for his money.

Liam Lawson - 9.5

Perhaps a tad too harsh on himself to say he could have done better than fifth on the road in qualifying, which was third after other penalties. In the race, faster cars like Verstappen and Piastri came through, although he did run a career-high second after a fast start and Lap 1, and fancied an attack on Antonelli. In the end, after Leclerc's penalty, beat both Ferraris for a fourth P7 in the last five races.

Nico Hulkenberg - 9

Missed all of Friday's running due to giving the car to Freddie Slater for FP1, in which it broke down and made him miss FP2. Stunning typical Hulkenberg guile to overcome Audi's lack of engine power and use the decent chassis to earn fourth on the grid once it shook out. In the same boat as Lawson that faster cars were always going to come through, and did well to pick his battles. Picked up a point despite a 10-second penalty for gaining an advantage whilst off track when battling Colapinto. Felt harsh.

Oliver Bearman - 9

A guy who starts P6 and finishes P17 scoring so highly might be unusual, but Bearman was on for a much-needed healthy points score, until a 20 second pit-stop ruined his race. He was running ahead of Leclerc and Hamilton, who finished eighth and ninth before the botched stop - after which his race was all but over.

The bottom five

Valtteri Bottas - 5

Reflective of qualifying only after the threaded wheel-nut lead to him posting a DNS for the first time this year. Out-qualified Perez on pace before the Mexican took his engine penalty.

Sergio Perez - 4

Out-qualified by Bottas by nearly eight-tenths and didn't make much progress forward in the race. Did beat Sainz's Williams, which was a plus.

Gabriel Bortoleto - 3

In an admittedly tough qualifying, ruined his chances of emulating Hulkenberg's fourth on the grid by spinning at Juncao and thumping the barrier. An ideal weekend and conditions to make a statement - he made one of the wrong kind.

Carlos Sainz - 3

Was not on Albon's level all weekend, and struggled in the first stint in the race as he cooked the intermediates. Is eager for the season to end.

Lance Stroll - 3

Another DNF for Stroll, which of course, cannot be held against him, so his score is largely based off qualifying, where in Q1, he was 1.561s slower than Alonso in conditions which represented a chance for him and Aston Martin. Alonso took it, Stroll didn't - with the Canadian a handy driver in the wet as evidenced by his pole position at the 2020 Turkish GP.

title: Lewis Hamilton 'devastated' as Sao Paulo GP unravels after 'rocket' start
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has expressed his devastation at how his Sao Paulo Grand Prix unfolded after a stunning start and opening lap one rival branded a "rocketship start."

From 20th on the grid after taking a fresh power unit, in the tricky conditions on Intermediate tyres, by Turn 5 on the opening lap, Hamilton was passing the Haas of Oliver Bearman, who had started sixth, and ended the first lap in ninth place.

The launch of Hamilton and that of Max Verstappen from 21st off the grid were branded as "rocketship starts" by Gabriel Bortoleto, but by Lap 3, Hamilton had began to struggle and was passed by Verstappen as he slipped back down the order and out of the points.

After insisting with the team, Hamilton then became the first driver to pull the trigger for the slick tyres on Lap 15, climbing back up to ninth, before crucially missing the pit-entry late on when the rain returned as he was forced to stay out for another lap in the worsening conditions.

Climbing the hill, Hamilton then spun and thumped the barrier with the rear wing as he crawled into the pits for his intermediate tyres, as he came across the finish line in ninth place in his 400th grand prix - and was lapped for the first time since the 2022 Emilia Romagna Grand Prix.

Taking to social media, Hamilton expressed his devastation with how the race had panned out.

"Devastated by yesterday’s race, especially with how it ended. It started so well, but we struggled with the tyres and massive oversteer," he wrote on Instagram.

"In those conditions, it made things incredibly difficult. I pushed as hard as I could, but we just didn’t have the pace this weekend. We’ll work to understand why and come back fighting at the next race.

"The team worked so hard on the car all weekend and I’m grateful for every bit of that effort. Ultimately, this isn’t the race we wanted to deliver, especially to this crowd 🇧🇷🇧🇷🇧🇷❤️‍🔥 Brasil, thank you always for the energy and support.

"This place holds such a special place in my heart; the love you give to me I send right back to you."

Hamilton also congratulated his former Mercedes team on winning its ninth constructors' title after the race, and thanked fans for "sticking with us."

"Well done to Mercedes for winning the Constructors' Championship and the incredible year they’ve had overall. Truly deserved," he said.

"To everyone supporting us, thank you for sticking with us through the difficult days as well as the good ones. I feel that support, and I don’t take it for granted."

title: Explained: Why Lewis Hamilton mistakenly gave away track position in Brazil
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton unnecessarily surrendered a position to Oliver Bearman during the São Paulo Grand Prix after the Ferrari driver was investigated for leaving the track and gaining an advantage during an overtaking manoeuvre.

The seven-time F1 drivers' champion was battling with his compatriot during the opening lap of the race at Interlagos when the pair went wheel-to-wheel through Turn 5.

Hamilton attempted to overtake Bearman around the outside but was forced beyond the track limits as the Haas driver defended his position.

Despite completing the move, Hamilton subsequently handed the place back to Bearman while the incident was under investigation a few laps later, seemingly to avoid the possibility of receiving a time penalty.

However, the stewards ultimately determined that Hamilton had done nothing wrong and was entitled to retain the position, meaning his decision to relinquish it had been in error.

[Article continues below]

Why Hamilton escaped punishment

The incident was investigated for a potential breach of Article B1.8.6 of the FIA F1 Regulations and Appendix L of the International Sporting Code, relating to leaving the track and gaining an advantage.

After examining onboard footage, the stewards concluded that Bearman's defensive manoeuvre had left Hamilton with no option but to run off the circuit to avoid contact.

Crucially, they also determined that Hamilton already had enough momentum to complete the overtake, meaning he had not gained an unfair advantage by exceeding the track limits.

In their official decision, the stewards explained: "The Stewards reviewed in-car video evidence and determined that Car 44 was attempting an overtake on Car 87 at Turn 5.

"In defending the position, Car 87 moved to the right and Car 44 was pushed off the track to avoid a collision.

"Car 44 clearly had the momentum for the overtake and gained no advantage by going off the track.

"We also noted that the position was subsequently given back by Car 44. We therefore took no further action."

Although the stewards acknowledged that Hamilton had returned the position, their findings established that the original overtake itself had been legitimate.

Consequently, Hamilton's attempt to avoid a potential penalty instead cost him track position that he was under no obligation to surrender.

title: Isack Hadjar reveals near Red Bull wipeout disaster before Brazil podium
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has described how he nearly wiped out his Red Bull team during the late pit-stop at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

With the field on dry-weather tyres, rain began to fall during the closing stages of the race at Interlagos, prompting a rush for intermediate tyres to survive the final laps.

Hadjar was battling for a podium position and was able to bag a third third-place finish of the season for the team, with Max Verstappen in second.

However, during the change from the slicks to the inters, the Frenchman revealed that in the difficult pit-lane, he nearly wiped out his pit-crew.

"I could see he was challenging me a lot and I was on ice, and he was on ice as well," Hadjar said of the battle with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli as the stop approached.

"I nearly shunted into my pit-crew when boxing, but they did a fantastic job. They kept their calm and the pit-stop was fast, so a big thanks to the boys."

Reflecting on the rest of his race, Hadjar described the difficulties in managing the inter-to-dry tyre crossover.

"It was so, so difficult, so challenging, especially switching from the inter to the soft tyre," he added.

"It was extremely difficult, especially in the pit lane. You saw how tricky it was to drive, and then more rain at the end, so I am happy to be standing third today.

"But I need to make fewer mistakes because I could have avoided a little awkward situation with Max, so I just want to apologise because I think on that stint I could have kept it a bit more on the track."

title: Kimi Antonelli voices anger after 'no warning' race-deciding F1 spin
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has voiced his anger at his performance in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix after spinning out of the lead ahead of a potential win.

From second on the grid, Antonelli jumped pole-sitter Lando Norris at Turn 1 to lead through the first stint on the intermediate tyres, with Lewis Hamilton and Carlos Sainz triggering the change to slicks on Lap 15.

Norris pitted next time by on Lap 16, with Antonelli staying out, but as Norris had far warmer soft tyres, he was able to wipe out the gap to the new world champion and mount a challenge for the lead on Lap 19.

On Lap 20, under braking for Turn 1, Antonelli lost the rear of the Mercedes and spun into the run-off, handing Norris a lead he would not lose, with the Italian then complaining about an issue aboard his W17 after a further off at Turn 1 on Lap 24, although engineer Peter Bonnington signalled there was no issue and told his driver to "refocus."

Antonelli eventually crossed the line in fifth place in his first race as drivers' champion, as his team took the constructors' title for the ninth time.

However, post-race, Antonelli signalled his "anger" at his performance, and explained that there was "no warning" the spin was coming at the start of his third lap on the slick tyres when temperatures should have started to build.

"I am very disappointed with the race, and I am very angry, to be fair, but I am going to put this aside for now, because the team clinched the title - and they deserve it," Antonelli reflected to media, including RacingNews365, when asked if it was bittersweet to lose the win as Mercedes took the title.

"But talking about the race, it is very disappointing as we were going for the win and once I was able to get some temperature [in the slicks], I was getting into the rhythm.

"But the spin came, which is something I need to look at because I don't know why I lost the rear so quickly; there was no warning, nothing.

"But to be fair, when I put the soft on, I felt something weird with the car, so we need to check what happened, but it is a shame as we lost the race there."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli on Sao Paulo GP

When then asked further about losing out on the win in Brazil, Antonelli signalled his desire to conquer Interlagos in 2027.

"I really wanted to win in Brazil in front of this amazing crowd, and it would have been cool to finish with a win, but it is a shame that I missed out, and hopefully, next year, we'll come back stronger and able to win it."

title: Charles Leclerc pained by 'complete disaster' Ferrari in wet weather 'coin flip'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has described his Ferrari car as a "complete disaster" to drive in wet weather conditions after a challenging Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

The Monegasque driver started Sunday's race from 13th on the grid due to an engine-related grid penalty, while team-mate Lewis Hamilton was 20th, demoted for a similar infringement.

While Hamilton made strong gains in the opening stages, Leclerc could not progress forward in a similar fashion.

Leclerc noted that he was struggling to get his tyres up to temperature, which stagnated his progress.

"The execution was okay, but the pace in the first stint was horrendous," he said.

"Particularly at the start, we had so much struggle getting those tyres up to temperature, it's unbelievable.

"It's just undrivable. Lewis definitely found a way because he had an incredible start, but for me, it was just like driving on ice.

"Later on, I had the pace but we had very little free air, and we also lost a lot of time in the straights."

"The first stint was very poor, the second stint on the soft was actually pretty good. But not much free air.

"At the end, by being patient and making the right choice, we ended up in P7 behind the top three teams."

[Article continues below]

Although Leclerc crossed the line in seventh place, he was demoted to eighth after being served a five-second time penalty for a collision with Liam Lawson.

While it cost Ferrari and Leclerc two points, it made little difference in the fight for the constructors' championship, which was sealed by Mercedes.

Leclerc called on Ferrari to take a deep dive into its wet-weather woes going forward as he highlighted the frustrations he felt behind the wheel.

"There is so much to learn," he said. "For qualifying, there are things we can learn from and do better.

"For [the race], and still in qualifying, I felt like we are going into the rain and it's like a coin flip.

"Maybe we end up on the right side of things, or we end up on the [wrong side].

"It's just a complete disaster to drive. We've got a lot of work to do on that side."
